One evening Policeman Harris, of
Nyack, noticed two supposed boys on
street corner acting in a suspicious
manner. He kept his eyes carefully
upon them for some time, and when
they moved off toward the railroad
station he followed them. The officer
soon became convinced that they were
girls masquerading in male attire, and
it was evident from their actions they
were novices in the business. Finally
he overlook them and called themto
account, informing them he was an Off
Ger and could not allow. such thing to
go on. The girls burst into tears and
admitted their sex. They said they
lived in Tarrytown, directly across the
river, and for the first time in their
lives had started on an adventure, not
supposing that they would be detected.


They belonged, it was ascertained, to
well known and respectable families in
Tarrytown, and had donned their broth
ers' clothes for the purpose Of having
"some fun" They were very much
troubled over the thought of being ar
rested and their mischief being made
known, and it was evident that they
bitterly repented their actions. The
officer told the girls their course was
dangerous one, and that they must re-
turn to their homes with him, which
they was more than willing to do. The
ferrybOat had stopped running before
this hour, and Harris procured small
boat and rowed them over the river,
taking them to their homes and deliv-
ering them to their parents.


The fathers of the girls were so
pleased with the conduct of the officer
that they secured large boat, took the
boat of Harris in tow, and brought him
back. The girls were each about l6
years old, and in letter which the Off
Ger received from them they explained
their original plan. They said they
wanted to have some sport, not fearing
any unpleasant consequences, and came
over expecting to take an evening train
from here to New York, and then to
return home. They say they now real
ize their foolishness, and will never at
tempt the same thing again.

Casting his keen gray eyes around
him as he did so, he suddenly espied
the thin, cadaverous-looking young
fellow, dressed all in black broadcloth,
who was sitting next to me in the cir-
cle around the stove.


"Why, howdy, Lemmel?" the old
man said, in the heartiest way. I
hardly knowed yer. How's the folks?"


"P-pr-pretty w-w-well, M-M-M
J. Johnson," replied the young man,
suffering miserably, as he submitted
to the hearty misunderstanding which the
old man had reached across several of
us to effect.


"Finished yer schoolin' yet?" in-
quired he.


"Y-y-yes, s-s-sir," replied the young
man, with difficulty.


"Well, what bizness are we in now?"
asked the old fellow, eyeing the dress
of his young friend rather curiously.


"I-I-I'm studying for the M-M-min-
istry."


"Phew-ee!" exclaimed the old man,
a long whistle of intense surprise.
"Well, now, Lemmel," he said, after
awhile, "that's about the last line
of bizness I'd ever thought of at-
temptin' to tackle if I'd a been in yore
place. Whatever put it into yore
head?"


"I had v-ve-very st-st-strong
plans," the young man, with a slight
flush on his pale, weak face.


"You might 'a had 81 dozen calls'"
returned the old man dryly; "but if
I'd a-been you I'd be switched if I'd
a come."


An audible smile ran around the
circle at the old man's wit, which he,
however, never noticed. His young
friend made no response to his last
suggestion, whilst he continued, in a
dry, anxious tone:


"It beats me, Lemmel, to know how
you low, even concedin' the call, to
git through with the rest of the
bizness."


"Th-th-the L-L-Lord will p-p-put
the w-w-words into my
mouth," gasped the poor young fell-
ow, suffering worse than ever under
the keen gray eyes of the old man.


"He'll have to do more than that,
sonny," said the old man, pityingly,
after he puts 'em thar. He won't hev to send somebody else
along to pull 'em out."


The young ministerial candidate re-
tired to his state-room, and was seen
no more.

country around for 15 miles. This elevator
is 15 feet high, and looking from its top, peo-
ple upon the streets of the town seem almost
like pigmies. Everybody seemed busy, and
the numerous teams and people which
thronged the streets, made a very interesting
sight. Buddes block, the Drug Store and
post office, McIntoshs, Batesen g. Ayres,
Kelley & Hillhouse's stores, Hoover Bros
market, Sandli & Swenson's machinery ware-
house, also Chas. Taylor's machinery place,
McBrayen's Hotel, Tibbits' block, J. B. Mas-
ter's bakery, McVicar's restaurant, the Bot-
tineau Co. Bank, the public reading room,
the customs office, three large livery stables,
harness shop, boot and shoe shop, and a
great many other smaller buildings, including
printing offices, residences, etc., besides the
two elevators already mentioned, were all
conspicuous, and told the story of the enter-
prise and prosperity of our town in far bet-
ter terms than is possible for our lead-pencil
to do. Remember that the railroad has only
been here bare two months, and that six
weeks ago the present townsite was entirely
unoccupied, whereas there is now a thriving
and bustling town of 500 to 600 people.

The country around, with its immense
wheat fields, looked green and inviting, the
splendid rains having compelled nature to
put on her best and brightest looks. The
scribe, from his lofty position, drank in a few
mouthfuls of the pure, exhilarating air, for
which our territory is noted, and then with
one long look down the railway track, which
with its long line of telegraph poles, could be
seen for 15 miles away, making a very pretty
sight upon the level prairies, and seeming
almost to disappear in the skies, descended
again to terra firma, well satisfied with the
result of his observations.

Begin with your externals generally, and attend to your insides: it is only through the latter that you can get one, and vary some four miles an hour with an occasional burst at top speed, or by leaping over a fence, or climbing a tree, or do it with will, and remember that your aim is not to make your muscles big and hard, but to get good appetite, good digestion, and a mind clear and efficient. As for your muscular strength, other people will teach you how that is getting on, when by any chance you happen to enter into competition with them.


To be out of doors whenever possible—that is the first desideratum. To breathe deeply and slowly—a second. Third, not less than these is to rub the surface of the body with stiff flesh brushes after it has become heated with exercise and before you sit down to any sedentary occupation. This brushing, of itself, nourishes and invigorates the muscles better than most kinds of gymnastic exercise because it induces the blood to flow into them and renders them supple and tough. Moreover it purifies the skin, enables the pores to breathe and relieves the lungs. If for any reason you cannot get your daily allowance of open-air exercise, then double your allowance of flesh brushing, and you will not miss the exercise so much. In this sort of regimen is kept up till the age of twenty-six, after which you will not need to be envious of prominent gymnasts.


In speaking about it, some people seem to feel morbid attraction toward unhealthy food, and an unwonted ingenuity in getting hold of it, and it is impossible to reform them. Other people have similar instinct for what is simple and digestible in food, and they need no advice. Still others are like hogs, they eat promiscuously and to excess; but they have not the hogs' excuse that they can be turned into bacon. But certainly it is well to eat less rather than more, and to eat what the stomach can readily endure. Instead of what the energies of the entire system must be taxed to put in order, do not eat very cold or very hot things. Do not drink ice water or scalding tea. Do not mind tobacco so much as some people seem to do; you must first find out how much of this poison your liver can neutralize without overexertion—and never exceed it. You need not be teetotaler,


Of the vast multiplication of homes in modern times, there is still almost as much outdoor work out in it as you can. Move about briskly with your mouth shut, and at every breath take in as much air as you can held through your nostrils. Do not go out with the premeditated purpose of running miles as fast as you can and then coming home again. Football is the best lung and heart game in the world, and whatever is most like football—such as hockey, tag, baseball—are so far good. Your movements should be varied, prompt, unexcited, and so far as possible so that you are not aware of the extent of the kind of exertion you are making. Take your time. Saw and chop wood once in a while or row a boat or throw weights or have a go at wrestling; do a certain thing at a certain time; only do something each day, and be outdoors while you are doing it. At the end of the year do not ask yourself whether you have increased three inches in your girth, or around the arms and legs. Your tailor will attend to those matters; look for your cheeks, and brightness in your eyes: that you eat a good deal more than you used to do, and that what you eat seems to dissolve away and become imperceptible the moment you have swallowed it; that you are asleep five minutes after you are abed, and until five minutes of the time.

COMPROMISE PROBABLE ON THE BROTHERHOOD ASSISTANCE AND PERCENTAGE QUESTION.

NEW YORK, Nov. 1.—The many baseball gossips who loitered about the Fifth Avenue Hotel to-day were still speculating on the chances of the Brotherhood with the League and the percentage question. The impression gained ground that a compromise in both matters would be effected. Ten o'clock was the hour set for opening the convention, but it was noon before the delegates began formal proceedings.

It is believed that President Day, of the New York club, will offer resolution making the percentage 15 per cent, where the attendance is over 5000; and a guarantee of 5000 in other cases. It is probable that this guarantee and 20 per cent will be adopted. President Stearns, of Detroit, who has asked for 80 per cent, intimated to reporter that he would be satisfied with the latter figures; he says that Boston and Philadelphia oppose the plan.

Mr. Billings, of Boston, offered Mr. Stearns $12,900 for Richardson and Thompson, but was told that $20,000 would not buy them.

Speaking of the Brotherhood, Mr. Stearns said, "You must remember that the League is eight years old and the Brotherhood but six months. They will have to come down from their high horse and appear before the convention. In this case I think their demand will not be granted after more or less negotiation."

There was filed with President Young this morning a contract that William Gleason of the St. Louis club signed last night with the Philadelphias. A proposition to permit managers to arrange percentages may be sprung on the convention.

Barrie, of Baltimore, was caught on the fly between two players whom he was buttonholing. "Yes, I am at it," said he, "all the rest are of it, and if I don't do the same I'll get left."

Doescher, who was a League umpire last year, and blacklisted, was reinstated yesterday. As soon as this was done he signed a contract to umpire for the National League Association next season.

As has been remarked by the commentators, and as is apparent to careful readers, it would seem that some notion of the week of seven days was current among the people whose history is recorded in very early times, that is to say, at a date long preceding Moses or any of the books written by him. The proof of this is to be found in such passages as the following: Genesis, xxx, "where Jacob is desired by Laban to fulfill her week," that is Leah's week, in order that he might also receive Rachel. The week appears to express the time given up to nuptial festivities. So afterward in Judges, xiv, where Samson speaks of "the seven days of the feast." So also on the occasion of the death of Jacob, "Joseph made mourning for his father seven days" Genesis, xl, 10. But "neither of these instances, any more than Noah's procedure in the ark, do further than showing the custom of observing a term of seven days for any observance of importance." They do not prove that the whole year or the whole month was thus divided at all times and without regard to remarkable events. They do not indeed prove this, but they suggest the division as common and familiar and in some early period recognized an institution.

When, therefore, the children of Israel went down to Egypt for what proved to be a very long sojourn in that country, they possibly were familiar with the practice of dividing time by weeks, and at all events the notion of seven days as a convenient portion of time for the affairs of life would not seem altogether strange to them. It is exceedingly probable that on arriving in Egypt they found the week established by the practice of the country. It will be observed that it was in Egypt that Joseph mourned seven days for Jacob; and it is possible, though there seems to be no necessity to assume the fact, that in so doing he was conforming to the custom of the country, as he did with regard to the embalming and cherishing of his father. But independently of any such consideration, it would seem highly probable that the Israelites found themselves in Egypt among people who divided the time by weeks of seven days. We know that they did so at a later period; why might they not have commenced as early as before the sojourn of the Israelites? The Egyptians were, in fact, people very likely to be advanced in such matters as this; order and government, both ecclesiastical and civil, were undoubtedly in a remarkable state of perfection at the time to which reference is now made, and it would seem much more probable than otherwise that so convenient an institution as the subdivision of the month into short periods had already been established. It may be noted with reference to the number seven and its recognition in some form or another as a special number among the Egyptians, that we have incidental evidence in the dream of Pharaoh; the special form of the dream, as presenting seven fat and seven lean kine, may be supposed to have been connected with some familiarity in Pharaoh's mind with the number seven during his waking hours.

And as regards the Israelites, it may be observed that the period of seven days is introduced into the most solemn event of their Egyptian sojourn, namely, the ordinance of the Passover. "Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses; for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel." — IN, Bishop of Carlisle to The Contemporary Review.

other in making your stay pleasant.

Here in British Columbia lived those men, farther from civilization than Ken lucky was from Philadelphia, and when I came and saw how they are living, the gilt of the romance was brushed off. Exiles perhaps from the human race, they have wandered off to the wilderness to die, and have lived on and on, and here are yet found old and mysterious. Some are sailors who were thrown on the shores of the western coast, or who deserted, and have found their way here, and never returned. Some are of that mysterious race of gold hunters who thirty and forty years ago ransacked all the western world for the precious metals. They are scattered far and wide now. The most of them are dead. Some yet live, and those who are of a peculiar class have met them in many a wilderness where I had thought that no one but I had ever been. mons while working in the corn

paid ministers enough to live on 7

bright feature, and that is the ad.
miration that all must feel for the

Yesterday the bonding of the land for the new reservoir was completed, and this afternoon the representatives of the Water Company and the Finance Committee of the City Government with the City Solicitor will meet at the Mayor's office to perfect the contract which will probably be presented to the regular monthly meeting of the City Government Monday night for ratification.

young and the assembly an experiment.
And yet it was not the same old steamer, for
the name at least was new, and so freshly
painted and overhauled and FURNISHED from
stem to stern was the boat that there was
nothing except the familiarity of its general
outlines to suggest its identity with the afore-
time "Moulton."


At the very outset I was brought face to
face with the unpleasant fact that there is no
longer competition among the steamers on
the lake, for instead of a couple of steamers
at the Lakewood wharf screeching for pas-
sengers, we found the Cincinnati gliding ma-
jestically away from the dock, although our
train was only five or eight minutes late. It
was accordingly over an hour later when
we were taken in out of the rain by the re-
juvenated and rechristened "Moulton."


The trip up the lake was varied by race
between the "Nightingale" as the Moulton
is now called, and a passenger train on the
new Chautauqua Lake railway, a fea-
ture which would have been pro-
nounced novelty only a short year ago. The
train went faster than we did of course, but
it made frequent stops, allowing us to make
up the distance lost; so that for a long time
we kept pretty nearly abreast of each other.
At length the engine gave a defiant little
snort and disappeared for good around a
wooded promontory.


The only other innovation during the trip
was a stop at the Long Point Gardens, where
a pensive-looking elephant was trying to
stand like a hen on one leg because the at-
mosphere was so cold and dank; while a
number of gaudily-painted menagerie cars
were disposed about the grounds in such a
way that their backs were toward the water.


My errand at Chautauqua was to obtain
both sides of the controversy between the
management and the cottage owners—a ques-
tion in which I had not the remotest personal
interest—and to forecast as carefully and
fairly as I could the future of Chautauqua in
view of the grave troubles which are now
threatening the peace and prosperity of the
assembly.


In order that the reader may have just the
amount of data that I had that evening as I
trudged up from the landing in the rain it is
necessary that I should go back and review
in the briefest, baldest way possible the agi-
tation and litigation which have character-
ized the present season here thus far, with an
occasional reference to the past. This histo-
ry may be surveyed in steps and epochs for
the sake of convenience as follows:


I. Eleven years or so ago about twenty or
twenty-five cottage-owners voted at a meet-
ing to put themselves under the rules and
protection of the association and to abide by
the ten per cent. tax levied upon gross re-
ceipts from boarding and lodging which the
association imposes on new lessees. These
cottage-owners were here by virtue of old
camp-meeting leases made out prior to the
institution of the assembly.


II. Era of subdued grumbling and protes-
tation on the part of cottage holders.


III. Early in June of the present year a
petition signed by ninety cottage-owners is
presented to the trustees asking for relief
from the tax of ten per cent, and suggesting
tax per bed as more equable.


IV. Early in July supreme Writs are served
upon six of the leading cottage-holders on
the grounds, Mrs. Dawson of Cottage Home,
Mrs. Scott of Longfellow cottage, Mrs. Rue
of Gale cottage, Mr. Beaujean, Mr. Blanch-
ard and Mrs. Glen, notifying them that in
twenty days they would have to appear and
answer certain complaints against them.


V. July 10 injunction served upon Mrs.
Dawson restraining her from keeping board-
ers for hire.


VI. July 27. Injunction dissolved.


VII. Cottage-owners—a double-barreled affair, ending
in a big row. The meeting gets so turbulent
that it is abruptly adjourned by the manage-
ment faction, and DR. Vincent marches out
of the room with the remark, "All loyal,
law-abiding Chautauquans will follow me."
The majority stay and Messrs. Wade and
Gale organize new meeting, in which cot-
tage-owners vote to rescind the original
agreement. Arrest of Wade and Gale or-
dered by President Miller.


VIII. August 11. Hearing of the case
against Wade. No complaining witness
appears.


Bemus served with warrants and gave
bail in the sum of two thousand dollars each.
Damage demanded on the ground of false
and malicious arrest in the sum of five thou-
sand dollars from each defendant by Messrs.
Gale and Wade.


I dropped into the first cottage that came to
me as I hurried up Miller avenue, and as I ate
my supper began pumping the landlady after
a careless fashion on the question of all-ab-
sorbing interest to every cottage-owner at
present. Said she: "I have not taken any
open part in the war myself. The manage-
ment send me guests frequently and of
course I hate to seem ungrateful. I suppose
if I hadn't some interest at stake in this way
I should feel as Mrs. Dawson, Mrs. Scott,
Mrs. Rue and many of the other cottagers
do."


"Are supplies much more expensive on the
grounds than at Jamestown for instance?"


"No," was the reply, "not as a rule. Some
things cost more. Some kinds of meat
which cost a shilling at Jamestown cost fif-
teen cents here, and vegetables are considera-
bly dearer. On the other hand sugar, tea,
coffee and some kinds of meat are quite as
cheap as at Jamestown. Milk is six cents on
the grounds unless you get a quantity of
tickets, and four cents just outside."


This statement of the expensiveness of
supplies I confirmed by subsequent inquiries
at other cottages.


I next proceeded to the Dawson cottage,
where I found Mrs. Dawson ill in bed, but
willing to give her side of the controversy
between herself and the management. She
is a woman of extraordinary shrewdness, an
exceedingly fluent talker, and quite equal I
should judge to pleading her own case in
court if she should not choose to hire a law-
yer. She has been prominent in Chautauqua
county during the last twenty years as an
evangelist and leader in temperance and mis-
sionary work. Said she:


"Of course I am distressed by this notori-
ety, but it has been forced upon me and I
must now defend myself or else seem to have
been in the wrong. We cottage owners are
rebelling at the ten per cent. tax because in
the first place it is a burden which many of
us find very onerous, and secondly because
it is illegally required of us. If we had the
vote it would be voted off. And we did."

regular officers?"

1.—THE Riddleberger advocates who insist on the sanctity and inviolability of the eleventh amendment delight in quoting the views of minority of the Supreme Court of the United States, as though the minority's opinion constituted the law of the land. The Constitution and the laws of the United States are just what the majority of the Supreme Court declares them to be, and should be respected and obeyed as such until that court finds reason to reverse itself. The character, learning, ability, and honesty in the minority is of no import; it is the majority that rules and makes the law under our system of government. Besides, it is quite certain that the Riddlebergerites would have claimed all these virtues for their minority had the Chief Justice and his dissenting associates been in the majority, and vice versa.

The Supreme Court made the DRED SCOTT decision, but the opponents of slavery never rested until the Constitution was changed and slavery abolished. That was an undertaking indeed. We in Virginia have no need to undertake any such work as that, inasmuch as the Constitution is already on our side. It might be said that all of the fifteen articles of amendment to the Federal Constitution were added to that instrument in order to protect the people or the States from what it was known would be the decisions of the Supreme Court, or from what had already been the decisions of that tribunal.

Our contemporary teaches sound doctrine. But the present bench of Justices is one of the cankers of a sectional war. It is not an impartial tribunal. It is not Federal court. It is not even a national court. It is a sectional court. It is a partisan court. There is upon the bench not one Democrat properly so called, the only pretended Democrat there being an appointee of Mr. LINCOLN's, more or less. There is not one man upon that bench who was not a sectionalist owing his appointment to that fact. WAITE and MATTHEWS—two from Ohio, and not one from twelve southern States—not one from even Maryland or Delaware—no one from a seceding State. One each from the new States of Iowa and California, but none from old Virginia. New York, Massachusetts, and New Jersey, three Justices, but not one Justice from single one of the late Confederate States. Justice WOODS, now dead, was really an Ohio man charged to Georgia, where he was, so to speak, mere carpet-bagger.

The present Supreme Court is therefore an exceptional body. We are bound to submit to its decisions but that fact does not preclude us from doing all that lies in our power to restore that tribunal to its ancient condition. At least three of the nine justices ought to be southerners, and at least four of them ought to be Democrats.

It is impossible to blind the eye of the southern people to the fact that the Supreme Court of the United States is a sectional, partisan, unfairly constituted tribunal.

James R. Fulton Post No. 257, Garden City, has adopted the following resolutions:

Whereas nearly a quarter of century has passed away since the last gunshot was heard at Appomattox when the conquered Lee surrendered his shattered army to the hero Grant; and

Whereas all over our country are seen the manned and crippled soldiers of the Army of the Republic who dared their breasts to the storm of war that the life of the Nation might be saved; and

Whereas there are many of the widows and orphans of our late comrades who are turned out to the cold charity of the world to seek a livelihood with but slender means at their command; and

Whereas the Congress of the United States, recognizing the claims of those veterans living, and the widows and orphans of those of our comrades who are now no more, passed what is known as the Dependent Pension Bill; and

Capitolian-Advocate.


Our esteemed contemporary of the Shreveport
Times is stretching his ingenuity to the Ut
most in endeavoring to make the Boatner
campaign an offset to the Hunt movement.
After acknowledging the support given by
Gen. Nichols to Mr. Hunt's candidacy, he
then makes the reckless statement that Gov.
McEnery supported Mr. Boatner. Unfortunately
for our contemporary, the beautiful
fabric he has woven is not of silk; in
fact, the threads are of spider webs and won't wash.
In the first place, the Hunt movement was
organized by a self-constituted committee
who made out a list of citizens whom they
called in conclave. At their conclave, these
citizens nominated Mr. Hunt as the candidate
of the Reform Democracy. All this they
did without a shadow of authority from the
Democratic organization. That was the
movement for which Gen. Nichols took the
stump. The circumstances were entirely
different in the Boatner contest. In
that case, a convention was assembled com-
posed of delegates elected under the auspices of
the Democratic Congressional Committee.
At the organization of that Democratic Con-
vention, a dispute arose which resulted in a


split. Each of the contending wings of this
convention nominated, the one, Mr. Hunt,
and the other, Mr. Boatner. It was an un-
fortunate dispute that Gov. McEnery and all
other good Democrats regretted, and it is
historical fact that he neither took the stump nor
voted for either of the rival candidates.

The surrender of the sixteen who left the reservation, eight of whom are in the guard house at San Carlos, put an end to the difficulty which came very nearly being extremely serious. At one time there were all the way from a thousand to thirteen hundred of the Indians who were on the point of leaving the reservation, but the timely arrival of General Miles and staff set matters right. From General Miles' observations the trouble was caused by the superstitions of the Indians. It appears that recently about a hundred of the children sickened and died, and shortly after the earthquakes came and other little things occurred which gave them gloomy forebodings. These feelings were worked upon by the medicine men, and the result was that over a thousand left their place on the reservation, and had camped forty miles away. Here they held meetings and orgies every night, and the medicine men had all of them worked up to a state bordering on frenzy, when General Miles appeared. The medicine men then changed their course, and, by considerable talk and persuasion, the Indians were quieted down and returned to the place where they belong. Their object was to leave the reservation and return to their homes. The sixteen who left the reservation were closely pursued by Captain Wendy and Lieutenant Johnson and after the Indian camp and animals were captured in the mountains about two hundred and fifty miles south they concluded that the safest thing to do was to return and give themselves up. When the camp was captured the Indians escaped by climbing down over the rocks, without taking anything along with them. They were closely followed by the troops on their way back and reached San Carlos just before their pursuers. Eight of the ringleaders were imprisoned in the guard house and will be tried by court martial under the direction of Captain Pierce. An investigation of the outbreak and its causes is going on at present and until it is concluded it is not known what course will be taken with the other eight. During their expedition the Indians, it is reported, killed two white men, but did not steal any great amount of stock.

General Miles said there was no truth in the rumor that they were about to attack Globe City. Indians never attack a city or thickly populated settlements, and so far as he could learn, they had no thought of such a thing. They were gone from the reservation from 10 to 15 days, and during that time travelled about 450 or 500 miles, going in a southerly direction about 250 miles. At the present time there are about 5000 Indians on the reservation belonging to the Yuma, Mohave, Tonto, White Mountain and San Carlos tribes of the Apache nation. There was no disaffection among any of those who remained at their settlements, and at the present time there is no fear of another occurrence and there will not be recurrence if the recommendations of General Miles are adopted.

SEC. 1. It is ordained by the Council of the City of Springfield, Ohio, that there be levied and assessed on the lots and lands in the Taylor street sewer district, or sewer district No. 3, according to the valuation, a special tax of one-half mill to pay the cost and expense of constructing the York street extension of the Taylor street sewer in said sewer district, provided for by ordinance passed August 10th, 1887, together with the interest on the bonds issued to provide fund to pay for said sewer.

Chicago, 2. Aug. — Eine große Versammlung der German Roman Catholic Seminars wird am 6. September in Chicago stattfinden. An einer großen amerikanischen Katholiken-Versammlung, die vor mehreren Jahren in dieser Stadt eine Konferenz und beißen wurde, ist der Aufruf der Deutschen Versammlung zu richten; Pastor Wilhelm Kappart aus St. Louis, Mo., Frederick Heues aus St. Louis und Wilhelm Kaiser aus Milwaukee wurden mit den einleitenden Schritten beauftragt. Diese katholischen Konferenzen (die Katholikentage) sind in Deutschland seit langer Zeit üblich, aber dieses Mal im September wird die erste sein, welche als solche in den Ser. Staaten stattfindet. Wie erwartet, wird der hauptsächliche Zweck der Co. BENTON in einer Erörterung der Differenzen zwischen den deutschen und irischen Katholiken bestehen. Die deutschen Katholiken in Amerika ertragen, dass jede Art von den hochmütigen Irern der Kirche der sich an die Vorherrschaft der Irer gegen die Deutschheit versucht oder versucht. Gleichzeitig wurde in Rom erhoben, und die Congregation der Propaganda hat hier entschieden, dass die deutschen Katholiken in den Ser. Staaten auf die anmelden werden mit ihren religiösen Ansichten. Die Contention soll dazu beitragen, die Stimme der deutschen Katholiken vor Augen zu führen, und Schritte ergreifen, um ihre Erweckung zu fördern. Man schätzt, dass circa 100,000 deutsche Katholiken in den Ser. Staaten befindlich sind. Betreffs Fragen der deutschen Sprache in Schulen und Schulen wird die Contention feine neue Forderungen erheben. Es wird beabsichtigt, dass die Versammlung auch die Arbeiterfrage behandeln und Schritte treffen soll, um respectable Irern besser Organe zu geben, um sie vor den gefahrlichen Einflüssen zu bewahren.

Das Glaubwürdigste ist der Wortlaut des Aufrufs der Glaubens abhaltenden Contention: gegen Interessierte, die die Aufgabe haben, die vert. allgemeine amerikanisch-deutsche Katholiken, Versammlung zu rufen. In Folge dessen tritt an uns die neue Bitte heraus, die amerikanisch-deutschen Katholiken der Ser. Staaten, gleichsam, ob dieselben einen katholischen Verein aus geben oder nicht, in dieser Versammlung einzuladen. Dieselbe wird am Dienstag, den 6. September, abends um 8 in der Großen Halle D-Salle in Chicago, Ill., erhoben werden. Die katholische Versammlung habe die große Aufgabe, das katholische Berufsleben zu pflegen, die katholische Interessen im öffentlichen und sozialen Leben zu fördern und die Kirche bei den, ihr Asser einzuführen und nützlich zu machen. In dieser Zeit ist eine Zeit großer Tätigkeit, eine Zeit, in der das katholische Volk aller Arten belebt und erneuert. Deshalb wollen auch nir, amerikanisch-deutsche Katholiken der Ser. Staaten, mit eintreten in den bl. Kampf für Arbeit, Freiheit und Recht. Wichtige Fragen treten an uns heraus; die Arbeiterfrage ist nie eine leichte Frage über unseren sozialen Zuständen; die Frage berührt die heiligen Rechte der Familie und Kirche; eine politische Organisation für die katholische Presse ist ein Bedürfnis; das der, einmige Sinn, nur die gemeinsame Grundlage der irischen Nationalität und der Katholiken Zusammengehörigkeit sich findet, muß es den Betrieb unserer Zeit aufpassen, wenn die Wahrung des bl. Gutes auch an uns gehört, insofern: wie wir besser die ehrenbare Bereicherung ausnutzen, damit sie nicht unheilvolle Einflüsse an dem haben. Zugehör der Erf der Zeit und die Bedeutung der heute Streit, Familie und Gesellschaft bergehenden Fragen dieser ersten allgemeinen amerikanisch-deutschen Katholiken Versammlung reicht viele Teile aus allen Staaten der Union zu ihm.

they are by the faces presented of those
with whom you may be acquainted.
Every artist who is capable Of repro
ducing a landscape cannot do the same
for the face. Besides calling for special
qualities, or talents, true facial expression
requires long experience. One must
learn to master a mans characteristics ut
a glance. BY study and observation the

mans face constitute expressions; what
is the proportion or length of his nose to

tic it exposes most strongly. The sue
cessful portrait painter, like the poet, Ia
born, not made. But one who could not
make his mark in line might by applica-
ton achieve a moderate success. To be
caricaturist requires still other talents.
One must have the comic idea blended
with the knack Of reproducing express
sions. There are very, very few success.
full caricaturists, considering the number
who aspire to be considered in that light.

altogether. The modern tendency is
clearly in the direction of curing diseases,

free will. It is found that the majority
of people who die at an advanced age were
in the habit of taking very little medicine.

yet to be seen. We are probably just on
the threshold. Half century may show

About now the political ball is beginning to roll. Committee meetings are being called, conventions held, and politicians generally are arranging their shoulders for the fall campaign. The Democrats being in power, are taking the initiative step in the move, and hence at this time more interest accrues in their action. It would not do, they think, however obnoxious may be the President's civil service policy, or his self-will and stubbornness in the matter of appointments, to pass administration by unnoticed; to do so would be a strong card in the campaign, so they have set about passing flimsy resolutions hoping to delude the unthinking into the belief that the party is a happy family and that the honest and lawful administration of the government to President is in perfect accord with the views and desires of the rank and file of the party. Time will soothe the anger, but it takes a long time, and repentance in all probability will reap forgiveness, but as the President has not changed his policy it is not reasonable to suppose dislike of him has in the last subsided, however anxious politicians may wish to so make it appear, and as he has not repented it is fair to presume his sins are not forgiven. responding period Of last year. In

ae increase Of 1854 pounds. The net

railroads and the establishment of a
market in Great Falls, with rates

good results.

The gentlemen who are interested in the affairs of the Republican party are depending too much on the momentum of that old and respectable institution to carry it successfully through the next campaign. We should have supposed that their experience in 1854 would show them in danger of such a reliance: It certainly ought to be plain to them that that danger is very much greater now than it was then. The momentum on which they trusted then has so far been insufficient that their chariot was brought to a dead standstill, and it remains to be seen whether, on the whole, it has not in the meantime gone back rather than forward. It should be clear to any attentive observer that the motives that might very fairly have been expected in 1854 to induce voters who had previously acted with the Republican party to continue to do so will not be so strong next year as they then were.

In the first place, there was then still lingering and exerting a very considerable influence the negative motive for cooperation with the Republicans supplied by the fear that the accession to power of the Democratic party would in some way impair the results of the war, lessen the security of the enfranchised slaves, open the way to extravagant claims on the Treasury from the South, and establish generally mischief and supremacy of the late rebel element at the Government. This fear has not been realized. The Southern question was seen by all rational men to have disappeared from national politics when President Arthur omitted all reference to it in his message to Congress in 1881; but the very sincere though rather vague sentiment to which it had given rise undoubtedly survived in 1884 and a sense of it survives, and will sway a good many thousand votes next year but it is no longer decisive, as Senator Sherman will discover should he continue his desperate effort to raise it to the dignity of an issue.

Added to this fear of the Democratic advent to power was the other, much more reasonable, that the policy of the Government as to the currency would be weakened and disturbed by an administration of that party. Business men in all parts of the country, but particularly in the large centres of commerce and finance, knew very well how very delicate was the situation of the country as to the currency, how great was the peril latent in the forced circulation of Government notes, the forced coinage of silver dollars and the arbitrary practice only indirectly authorized by law by which the gold reserve was maintained in the Treasury and the Government payments were made in gold. They felt that it would involve great risk to put the Treasury into the hands of men not bound by the traditions then prevailing. They knew that little ignorance, little temerity, even little honest narrowness, where such vast consequences depended upon the use of most difficult and undefined discretion, might bring us to silver payments, seriously injure the credit of the Government and plunge the country into confusion. This fear is absolutely dissipated. The traditions of the Treasury have not been broken but they have been in many ways strengthened, and the discretion by which the enormous interests affected by the Department have been protected has been used with greater wisdom, firmness and courage than ever before. The Treasury is safer now than at any time since 1857.

If candid consideration of the facts we have mentioned—and they are, of course, but a few of those bearing on the situation—will show that victory will not come to the Republicans next year by merely waiting for it, in the trial before the people of the question, shall there be change in the National Government the burden of proof is clearly shifted. Those who insist on the change will have to show, first, that the change ought to be made in their favor. At present the Republican leaders are singularly neglecting both these tasks.—N. J. Lines, (Ind. Rep.)

A meeting in the interests of Whitehead lecturer of the National Grange. Which he press of the State has made a public affair, was held in the large hall upon the fair grounds of Oxford County Agricultural Society, on Tuesday, Aug. 9th. Mr. Whitehead, lecturer of the National Grange, the patrons of Oxford County, than whom none are more earnest, elective or intelligent in their efforts to enhance the welfare of those engaged in agriculture, and believing that in no way can this be done more successfully than by such organization as the Grange. Of the country, to the farmers, such patrons therefore naturally expected that those living in so good a farming region as that at the fair grounds, would since a desire to know what the Grange is, what its principles are, and what its aims to accomplish; and just as naturally it was expected the Lecturer of the National Grange would be one fully qualified to illustrate and elucidate and to clearly and forcibly set forth its principles, purposes, and what it has already attained.

The meeting was fine, but the attendance was small. Several reasons may be given why some were not there, but the conviction forces itself upon us that lack of interest was the one that had most weight with the greater number that kept away. In my opinion, for a moment right here, to me it is quite certain that farmers are making progress in many ways that do make up a successful and pleasant life, and yet there are many who move on in the same old way, old ruts, as they are called, whose life goes hard, whose farms are far from being as productive as they ought to be, whose methods and practices are not such as to bring remunerative crops nor such as good, prosperous farmers pursue. And such farmers are the ones who grumble, and fault, and condemn the farms, and, in fact, everybody and everything, while the fault is in themselves. The whole press of the country now devotes part of its columns to agricultural interests, while that more especially devoted to the farming calling is ably conducted, and is aided with the best thoughts by those who have made farming successful by intelligent practice. Yet, lacking the practice of too many of these grumblers, they do not read. And whatsoever pains our Board of Agriculture may take to hold meetings, such grumbling farmers stay away, or if they attend, no impression is received. Now while they are grumbling and growing, the world moves, and farming goes onward, growing with other growths. The era of progress has gone by, leaving many, woe betide, for no one's fault but their own, might have gone forward, if they had, but those have who, availing themselves of the opportunities presented, and who by putting the knowledge gained by such opportunities into practice upon their farms, have gained all agricultural success, and the comforts and delights of life are theirs and those whose happiness is so largely dependent upon them.

The order of patrons has always been instituted not alone to meet the wants of the more progressive farmers, nor yet mainly for such, but for all, and to none does it hold out more helping hand, to none the inducement offered greater than those who, for one reason or another, fail to reach that measure of success in life that brings the highest enjoyment. It is for such and to benefit them that our best patrons are working, and for this reason it is that lecturers are in the field to show the objects sought for, the advantages to be obtained, and what has actually been gained, that adds something to the large class. Mr. Whitehead, the National Lecturer, came here for this purpose, and was expected. He told of much that had been gained by organization, and much more that can be by guidance, and how futile and feeble are our efforts when working alone. So far to gaining any state of national advantages, a report of the lecture of Mr. Whitehead will not attempt but wish to draw the lesson he attempted, which is that to our fault we do not avail ourselves of every opportunity to gain information relative to our calling, or profession as it is, and may with propriety be called. We may just well settle down to the fact that an era of low price is upon us, and that it is only by putting such a degree of intelligence into our farm practices as will enable us to produce crops as pront under such conditions, things will bring us success, remembering that low prices mean less comforts to the great class of laboring people.

The following letter to the Voice from
Thomas Stevens the famous bicyclist, who
adds another testimonial from the great
travellers in favor of total abstinence:


I incidentally learned the other day that my
article, "The Drinks of All Nations," that appeared in the Sun October 8, has created the
impression upon the minds of some that I
personally advocate the use of alcoholic
beverages. I therefore beg that you will give
me sufficient space to "stand corrected."


What the Sun rightly entitled my curious
observations must not be mistaken as personal advocacy of liquor drinking, as against
temperance, even when viewed from the
"nation" standpoint. For the benefit of those
readers who cannot be expected to know anything about newspaper writer's position,
I would point out that he has small choice of
subjects. He has to sink his personality out
of sight entirely. Like the man who raises
vegetables for the market, it is imperative
upon him to produce varieties that meet with
the readiest sale.


I see the opposite side of the question producing
points quite as plausible as my observations
that nations who drink the most alcohol do
the best fighting. As the Chinese philoso-
pher said, when they were whipped by the
allied forces, "the ability of the foreign devils
to fight doesn't establish their superiority
now."


Turning from the national observations
of the Sun article to an individual traveller's
view, I may say that the views of Henry M.
Stanley, on the temperance question, are
fully verified by my own experiences. He
believes, and so do I, that alcohol as a beverage should be avoided, but that a mild stimu-
lant—a glass of claret, or a s'peg"—in the
evening, after a fatiguing day, is not a bad
thing. Its use in this manner relegates it to
its proper sphere as medicine, as distinct
from beverage. That alcohol is sometimes
useful in medicinal practice, few, I suppose,
would care to dispute. It is also an excellent
thing for preserving tarantulas and freaks of
nature.


From a social standpoint, I don't think
anybody needs to be told that a community
of thoughtful and rejecting temperance peo-
ple—"Prohibition cranks," even, if you will—
would be a vast improvement upon the
heterogeneous elements that now abound al-
most everywhere in our country.


While I am not quite prepared to take the
extreme views that some take, I am in strong
sympathy with the mission of such men as
John B. Gough and kindred spirits. I want
it to be distinctly understood that I am a
strong advocate of temperance. I attribute
my remarkable immunity from sickness un-
der the most trying climatic conditions to
the fact that I have, all my life, been prac-
tically—though not professedly so—a tota-
l abstainer. As a matter of fact, I was
a Blue Ribbon wearer for over ten years, and
I might just as well be one now as then.


NEW YORK, THOMAS STEVENS

portions. Frederick Krupp was the discov-
erer of the method of casting steel in very
large masses. He sent to the London Exhi-
bition of 1881 blocks weighing fifty German
quintals, which was regarded as a marvel,
but he has since cast blocks weighing more
than four thousand quintals. Herr Krupp
manufactured large number of articles
used for peaceful purposes, but his name is
more particularly associated with the gi-
gantic steel siege guns which the Germans
used with such terrible effect against the
city of Paris.


The steel works at Essen are the largest in
the world. They cover nearly five hundred
acres and employ seven thousand men. Two
hundred and forty steam engines, with a
power of 800 horses, are continually run-
ning. There are fifty steam hammers and
two hundred and forty furnaces, which con-
sume eighty thousand tons of coal yearly.
Krupp was at one time offered letters of no-
bility by the King of Prussia, but declined.

Perhaps the most successful of the minor editors of New York was the late Charles D. Keep, of the Wall Street News. He was an indefatigable worker and a singularly quiet and transformations man. Columns of "READING matter" appeared in the New York daily press continually about the personal and financial peculiarities of Charles D. Keep. It was all of complimentary nature, but every article adroitly pulled patent nostrum in which the editor was interested. He made more than $500,00 in less than ten years, and he established at least two admirable pieces of property—his paper and his patent medicine. Both were forced to success from a beginning that was practically nothing.


Perhaps the most notorious of the lesser editors is Paul Potter, a man who is in continual warfare and who has, nevertheless, the most amiable and hospitable nature in the world. He is a remarkable man. For several years he was at the head of the foreign department of the Herald. He received a very large salary and was far and away the most accomplished editor that the New York press has known. Potter is not only able to speak every tongue and dialect, but he is familiar with politics all over the world, and is able to twist cast iron dispatches from Buda Pesth, Moscow and Cape Horn into such trenchant English that even business men are attracted by them. There is a sharp, nasty, satirical vein in his character and when he gave this full swing in Town Topics it set the town agog for a time. Dramatic journalism is decent now. The survival of the fittest is exemplified again. It is a difficult task at best to force a weekly paper to success in New York nowadays, as the big thirty-page Sunday papers cover all available territory.
